manual.title: User manual
manual.intro: How the platform is worked, from the first sign-in to the last guest. Each chapter reads in a minute.

signIn.title: Signing in
steps: The end client and the staff sign in without a password: you type your email at /entrar and a six-digit code arrives.
The platform account and office administrators may also have a password, to get in on the days the mail is not moving. The link sits under the code field.
The code works ONCE and expires after ten minutes. If it runs out, ask for another.
The answer is the same whether the account exists or not: the system never reveals who is registered.
Sign out from the link at the top. On a shared computer, always sign out.

interface.title: The panel language
steps: Top right there are four buttons: العربية, Español, Português and English. Press yours.
The choice is saved on YOUR account, not the office’s: two colleagues at the same desk can read it in different languages.
Choosing Arabic turns the whole panel right to left, not just the words.
This does not touch the invitations’ language: that is decided per version, on the event’s page.

create.title: Creating an invitation
steps: /crear has six steps: language and event type, names, when and where, details, other languages, and review.
The preview on the side is the real invitation — the same component the guest will see. What you see is what gets published.
The event type decides the template and the colours. A memorial never uses the celebration template, and the form cannot force it.
The verse is chosen from a closed, verified list. There is no free-text field for a sacred text, deliberately.
Publishing needs a session and uses one event of your plan. The limit is checked on the server as you publish.

languages.title: The languages
steps: The language you pick in step 1 is the main one: the invitation is created in it, and it is the fallback.
In step 5 you can write the same invitation in the other languages. You write the text: nothing is translated for you.
The names, the date and the venue are the same in every version. Only the message and the verse change.
Each version has its own writing direction, its own numerals and its own public link.
You can also add a language later, from the event's page.
Each guest opens the version in THEIR language. Anyone without one gets the main version, and the guest list flags it in red.

guests.title: The guest list
steps: On the event's page you paste the list or upload a file. One line per guest: name, phone, language.
Commas, semicolons and tabs all work. If the first line is headers, it is detected on its own.
Pick the country code before importing: phone numbers are stored in international format.
A line with no name is skipped and counted. An empty guest is never imported.
Pasting the same list again duplicates nobody: guests are matched by phone, and by name when there is no phone.

send.title: Sending over WhatsApp
steps: Each guest has their own link, short and without the event's name, so forwarding it does not reveal whose wedding it is.
The button opens YOUR WhatsApp with the message already written. It goes out from your number, the one your clients know.
The message is in the guest's language, not the office's.
There is no per-message fee and no templates to get approved: this is not the WhatsApp API, it is your own WhatsApp.
A guest with no phone shows a link to copy and send however you like.

rsvp.title: Replies
steps: The guest answers on the invitation page itself, with no account and no password.
Opening the link records the date, so you can see who received it even before they answer.
The event's page sums up who is coming, who is not, and how many they bring.
The download button hands you the list as CSV with a byte-order mark, so Excel does not wreck the Arabic.
Every invitation has a calendar file, so the guest can save it to their phone.

image.title: The image
steps: Each invitation is rendered as a 1080×1920 PNG on the server, with the same layout as the page.
The image is stored the first time and reused. It is also the preview WhatsApp asks for when the link is shared.
Adding ?download=1 to the end of the image address downloads it instead of opening it.
If anything on the invitation changes, a new image is made on its own: the fingerprint covers everything that changes the drawing.

team.title: Team and permissions
steps: Each office sees only its own events. One office never reaches another's data.
There are four roles: superadmin, office admin, operator and organiser.
The operator creates and edits events and guests. The organiser only looks.
Billing and the team are managed by the office admin.
Permissions are always checked on the server: a button you cannot see is not a permission.

system.title: System status
steps: Only the superadmin sees it, because it names the configuration variables that are missing.
At the top, eleven checks: database, outgoing mail, payment gateway, encryption key, Chromium and the rest. Green is fine; red says exactly what is missing.
Below, the versions of everything running, read live from the machine.
The "Send a test email" button sends a real message to the superadmin and shows the server’s answer. It is the only thing that tells "misconfigured" apart from "the provider refuses the password".
The server accepting the message does not guarantee it reaches the inbox. If it does not turn up, check the spam folder before touching anything.
Updating packages is done from the console, not from there: the screen gives the exact commands.

mail.heading: Test outgoing mail
mail.intro: Sends a real message to the superadmin address. It is the only way to know whether SMTP works: the configuration can be complete and the provider still refuse the login.
mail.ok: Handed over to the mail server. Careful: accepting it does not guarantee it reaches the inbox — if it does not show up within a few minutes, check the spam folder.
mail.failed: The mail server refused it. Its answer, verbatim:

updates.heading: Updates
updates.intro: The versions above are the ones installed on this server right now.
updates.warning: Updating from the browser is deliberately not enabled: installing a package and restarting the service from a web page would be running code on the server from a signed-in session, and a bad version would take the site down with no way back. It is done from the console, with a backup.

hero.badge: Made for Lebanon · Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese and English
hero.titleLead: Your invitation, in each guest's own
hero.subtitle: Digital invitations for weddings, graduations and memorials. A web page, an image for WhatsApp and the replies — with nothing for anyone to install.

features.heading: Everything it takes to invite
features.subheading: No generic templates and no machine translation.

languages.title: Four real languages
languages.body: Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese and English. Arabic runs right to left across the whole card, with its own numerals and its own typeface. Each guest opens the version in their own language.

whatsapp.title: Sent over WhatsApp
whatsapp.body: Every guest gets their own link from the number their family already knows. No approved templates and no per-message fee.

rsvp.title: Replies that count themselves
rsvp.body: Guests answer on the same page, with no account and no password. You see who opened it, who is coming and how many they bring.

image.title: An image ready to share
image.body: The same invitation comes out as a 1080×1920 PNG rendered on the server. Download it, print it, or send it as it is.

verses.title: Verses checked by a person
verses.body: Qur'anic and biblical texts come from a fixed list a human has verified. A machine never writes them.

offices.title: Built for offices
offices.body: Each office sees only its own events, with its own team, plan and invoices. An event never crosses from one office to another.

steps.heading: Three steps
steps.subheading: From the guest list to the replies.

write.title: Write it
write.body: Five steps with a preview that is the real invitation, not a mock-up. Pick the language and the whole form switches to it.

send.title: Send it
send.body: Paste the guest list with their phone numbers. Each guest gets their own link over WhatsApp, written in their language.

track.title: Follow it
track.body: Who opened it, who replied and how many are coming. Export it to a spreadsheet whenever you need to.

showcase.heading: Two templates, two tones
showcase.subheading: One for celebrating and one for mourning. The event type decides which, never whoever fills in the form.

pricing.heading: Pricing
pricing.subheading: One event, or a whole office.
pricing.note: Payment in Lebanon is taken through Whish. Amounts are stored as whole cents: no decimal ever touches money.

benefits.free: 1 event and up to 50 guests. To try it out.
benefits.annual: 10 events a year, up to 500 guests each.
benefits.office: Unlimited events and guests, under your own brand.

guestApp.question: Does the guest have to install anything?
guestApp.answer: No. The invitation is a web link that opens in the phone's browser. No account, no password and no app.

languages.question: Do you translate the invitation?
languages.answer: Not automatically, and that is deliberate. You write the text for each language; we never transliterate a family name or paraphrase a verse. The names, the date and the venue are shared by every version.

payment.question: How is payment taken in Lebanon?
payment.answer: Through Whish. Payment is confirmed server to server: coming back to the success page is never proof that anything was paid.

print.question: Can I print it?
print.answer: Yes. Every invitation downloads as a 1080×1920 PNG rendered on the server — the same one the guest sees.

ownNumber.question: Do the messages come from my number?
ownNumber.answer: Yes. We open your own WhatsApp with the message already written, so it goes out from the number your clients already know.

closing.heading: Is there a wedding this season?
closing.body: Write the invitation, paste the list and send it today.

footer.tagline: Digital invitations in Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese and English.
